# Results

## Model Performance

To answer the research question of whether the bioelectrical plant
signal correlates with the participant's emotional state, three machine
learning model architectures are compared (RandomForest, XGBoost,
NeuralNetwork), each of them tested on two feature representations (raw,
session_norm), resulting in six combinations for each of the three
target variables: valence, arousal, and proxy emotion label.

Data recording resulted in a dataset including 284 windows from 15
participants. The evaluation was performed using a nested five-fold
cross-validation procedure grouped by participants, ensuring that no
participant appeared in both the training and test data simultaneously
and that the hyperparameter tuning never utilized information from the
test data used to evaluate how well the model performs. This ensures
that the reported values are reliable and avoids leakage. For statistical
validation, a permutation test with 200 label permutations was
additionally performed to assess how likely the obtained result would be
under the null hypothesis of "no correlation."

### Valence Classification

The target variable valence, determined by FER (HSEmotion), contains
three classes: negative, neutral, and positive. The classifiers predict
valence with accuracies between 36–43%. @fig-valence
represents all six combinations sorted by their f1 macro value.

![Classifier comparison: target variable valence.](figures/valence_comparison.png){#fig-valence width=80%}

Of the six (model, feature set) combinations compared, RandomForest on
the "session_norm" feature set performed the best with an f1 macro of
approximately 0.42. The permutation test confirms that this result is
statistically significant (p = 0.0050). Zero out of 200 random label
permutations matched or exceeded the result actually observed.
Therefore, valence is the target variable for which the plant signal
shows the clearest and most robustly validated predictability. In
addition, all three classes of valence were recognized with similar
accuracy. The RandomForest "session_norm" combination predicted the
three classes with an F1-score between 40-45%, which further emphasizes
this combination. In contrast to the emotion classification,
there was no significant bias toward a dominant class in this case. Averaged across all models, the effect of session
normalization increases the f1 macro scores by 0.031 for this target
variable. For RandomForest, the improvement compared to the raw feature
set of 0.068 is the highest and highlights the strongest individual case
across all target variables.

: Model performance by target variable {#tbl-perf}

| Target   | Best model            | Accuracy | f1 macro |
|----------|------------------------|:--------:|:--------:|
| Valence  | RandomForest (snorm)   |  36-43%  |   0.42   |
| Arousal  | NeuralNet (snorm)      |  32-37%  |   0.36   |
| Emotion  | RandomForest (raw)     |   42%    |   0.21   |

@tbl-perf summarizes the best combination per target variable.

The Direct Current (DC) level of the plant voltage drifts between
sessions, because of changes in temperature, CO~2~ baseline in the room,
etc. This is not related to the person's emotions but is background
noise from the measuring equipment. Therefore, it is important that the
most important predictors are shape- or amplitude-based, not
level-based, features, such as `plant_detrend_std` (standard deviation of
the plant voltage after the baseline drift has been subtracted) and
`hjorth_mobility` (indicating how quickly/frequently the signal
changes), while `plant_max` (the maximum plant voltage value within the
30-second window) is still part of the most important features. The
model therefore relies mainly on how the curve moves within the window,
not on where it lies overall. This is an indication that the model is
learning about the actual signal dynamics and not recognizing a session
based on its random baseline.

### Arousal Classification

The target variable arousal, derived from HRV (RMSSD) and the mean heart
rate, contains three classes: calm, neutral, and activated. None of the
classifiers are able to predict arousal better than random, as the
accuracies range between 32-37%, which is close to random (approximately
0.33) with three classes (see @fig-arousal).

![Classifier comparison: target variable arousal.](figures/arousal_comparison.png){#fig-arousal width=80%}

Nevertheless, NeuralNet on the "session_norm" feature set combination
performed the best at an f1 macro of approximately 0.36. The result does
not quite reach the threshold to be statistically significant
(p = 0.0547). The classification report concludes that all three classes
were classified with similarly low accuracy (F1 0.18-0.46) and no model
performs significantly better on any one class. However, it must be
noted that there is an unbalanced distribution of the classes: "neutral"
is clearly the largest class, with 115 out of 284 cases (approximately
40.5%), while
80 cases are labeled activated, and 89 calm. The approach of session
normalization is most effective and consistent for the target variable
arousal, improving the f1 macro scores of all three models by an average
of 0.035. As with valence, the same applies here: DC-invariant, shape-
and amplitude-based features, such as `plant_max`, `spectral_entropy`
(spectral disorder), `spike_rate_snorm` (frequency of transient
amplitude fluctuations, session-normalized), and
`hjorth_activity_snorm` (signal variance in the time window,
session-normalized), dominate the classification.

### Emotion Classification

Regarding our research question, our most important target variable is
emotion. Similar to the Circumplex Model [@russell1980], our emotion
label is created by combining the valence- and arousal-result, leading to
five classes: negative activated, negative calm, neutral, positive
activated, positive calm. The best-performing combination is
RandomForest on the "raw" feature set, with an accuracy of 42% and an f1
macro score of 0.21 (see @fig-emotion).

![Classifier comparison: target variable emotion.](figures/emotion_comparison.png){#fig-emotion width=80%}

This is the only case where the "raw" feature set performs better than
the "session_norm" feature set, contradicting the otherwise consistent
trend. Regarding the target variable emotion, there is a significant
class imbalance, as "neutral" dominates (177 out of 284 cases, F1
0.6-0.75). This is the reason why the accuracy of 42% appears so much
higher than the macro-F1 score of 0.21. Therefore, the model largely
predicts the majority class well while barely distinguishing the
minority classes (e.g. F1 0.08 for "positive activated"), as reflected in
the much lower macro-F1 of 0.211. So while emotion prediction is
statistically better than a random classifier, accuracy alone overstates
how much the model actually understands about emotional states. The
permutation test verified the statistical significance (p = 0.0149), but
it is weaker than for valence. As with valence and arousal, dynamics-based
features dominate the most important features for classification of the
emotional state.

## Correlation Analysis

![Confounding triangle (plant, valence, CO~2~) and the per-feature partial correlation with valence before and after removing CO~2~.](figures/co2_correlation.jpeg){#fig-co2 width=95%}

@fig-co2 summarizes the confounding triangle and the per-feature partial
correlation results discussed below.

The correlation analysis is conducted in two complementary variants. In
the raw analysis, plant features showed a weak but frequently
significant correlation with valence (mean $|\rho|$ = 0.140, significant
in 13 of 22 features), while the correlation between plant features and
CO~2~ concentration, evaluated at its optimal time lag (a change in
ambient CO~2~ is expected to affect the plant voltage only after a short
delay), was substantially stronger (mean $|\rho|$ = 0.420, significant in
18 of 22 features). CO~2~ itself was also correlated with valence
($\rho$ = 0.308, p < 0.0001). Together, these three pairwise
relationships form a plausible confounding triangle: CO~2~ correlates
with both the plant signal and valence, raising the question of whether
the plant-valence relationship is genuine or merely an artifact of CO~2~
acting on both variables independently. To test this directly, we
computed the partial correlation between plant features and valence
while controlling for CO~2~. If CO~2~ were the true driver of the
plant-valence association, this partial correlation should collapse
toward zero. Instead, it remained almost unchanged, with a change of
only -3% (0.140 -> 0.145) after CO~2~ control, and is not a confounding
artifact.

The session-normalized analysis provided further insight into the nature
of the CO~2~ effect. Once between-session variance (e.g., differences in
room climate across recording days) was removed, the plant-CO~2~
correlation (at optimal lag) dropped sharply to a mean $|\rho|$ of 0.101
and was no longer
classified as a robust, present effect. This indicates that most of the
raw plant-CO~2~ coupling reflects slow, session-level environmental
drift rather than a genuine within-session physiological interaction.
Despite this reduction, the plant-valence partial correlation remained
stable even after CO~2~ control within sessions (0.075 -> 0.074, a
change of only -1%), confirming the confound-rejection result at both
the between- and within-session level.
